title: The Glasshouse of the reservoir
premise: Jonah Montrose, a piano tuner who reads houses through their radiators and pipes, is hired to service the old reservoir glasshouse on the Montrose family estate — a house he grew up in as the foster child no one claimed. There he meets Ada Kessie, the last fluent speaker of Nsibidi-Olum, a dying language, who asks him to become her final student so that one untranslatable sentence — her mother's last words to her — will not die with her. As Jonah learns, he discovers the sentence is bound to his own buried history: the estate's patriarch silenced Ada's community to build the reservoir, and Jonah's foster years were part of that cover-up. To translate the sentence he must finally say what was never said aloud in the glasshouse, and the novel ends with him speaking it at Ada's deathbed — imperfectly, but truly — choosing belonging over inheritance.
about_author: Ivo Okafor is the pen name of a former acoustic engineer who spent a decade restoring pipe organs in decommissioned civic buildings across northern England. Their fiction explores how places remember what people are paid to forget.

chapters.title: The Tuning Fork Winter
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A quiet opening: Jonah tunes a dead woman's piano in a terraced house and hears, in the radiators, the argument that preceded her death. He keeps his ledger of unsaid things. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Commission from the Estate
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A letter arrives commissioning him to tune the conservatory piano at Hallow Reservoir House — the estate where he was fostered at nine. He accepts against his own instinct. Beat: dread braided with longing.

chapters.title: What the Pipes Remember
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Walking the grounds, he reads the house's plumbing like braille: additions, severings, a wing sealed since the flooding of the valley. The current heir, Charles Montrose, greets him with practiced warmth. Beat: the past as physical pressure.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Ada's POV introduced. Ada Kessie, eighty-one, lives in the restored Victorian glasshouse among salvaged plants from the drowned valley. She hears Jonah tuning and corrects his pitch by singing. Beat: two keepers of dead things recognizing each other.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She asks Jonah to learn Nsibidi-Olum before her memory finishes going; she has refused everyone else for forty years. He refuses too — then hears her hum a lullaby he somehow knows. Beat: the hook closes.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. First lessons: numbers, greetings, the word for 'reservoir,' which is also the word for 'grave.' Charles watches the lessons with polite unease. Beat: wonder shadowed by warning.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Flashback to his fostering: the silent dinners, the rule that he never ask about the valley or the families moved out for the water. His ledger habit began here. Beat: childhood silence explained.

chapters.title: Grammar of Grief
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada teaches the language's grief constructions — tenses for things lost. Her memory lapses begin mid-lesson; she calls Jonah by her brother's name. Beat: urgency enters the tenderness.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She reveals the task beneath the lessons: her mother's final sentence, spoken as soldiers cleared the village, which she has never been able to render into English. She will teach him everything so he can carry it. Beat: the stakes made explicit.

chapters.title: Charles's Archive
chapters.summary: Charles's POV. In the estate office, Charles finds his grandfather's correspondence about the compulsory purchases and the 'Montrose orphan placement' scheme — Jonah was placed deliberately, a living confidentiality clause. Beat: complicity inherited.

chapters.title: The Drowned Bell
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Low water in the reservoir exposes the village church tower; Jonah and Ada walk out to it. Underwater acoustics carry a half-heard bell. Ada names the street they stand above. Beat: awe curdling into horror.

chapters.title: Lessons Interrupted
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Charles offers Ada money to relocate to a care facility 'for her own good'; she declines in Nsibidi-Olum, and only Jonah understands the insult. Alliance forms between student and teacher. Beat: power shows its face.

chapters.title: The Radiator Speaks
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Repairing the glasshouse boiler, Jonah finds a child's tin box in the pipework: photographs, a valuation notice, and a list of placed orphans — his name on it. Beat: the house itself testifies.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Weir
chapters.summary: Jonah and Charles POV alternating. Jonah confronts Charles; Charles argues the family gave the boy a life, that some silences are mercy. Jonah hears his foster father's voice in Charles's. Beat: the temptation to stay silent, articulated well enough to shake him.

chapters.title: Memory Going Like Tide
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada's decline accelerates; she loses English first, retreating into Nsibidi-Olum entirely. Lessons reverse — now Jonah translates the world for her. Beat: role reversal, deepening love and fear.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence, Part One
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Ada, lucid at dawn, gives him the sentence whole. Its grammar has no subject — grief without an owner. He cannot parse it; every English rendering makes someone guilty or innocent, and it must be neither. Beat: intellectual crisis as moral crisis.

chapters.title: Breaking the Glass
chapters.summary: Climax begins, Jonah's POV. Charles moves to have Ada sectioned; Jonah plays the evidence — recordings, the tin box, the archive — to the family solicitor and the valley's surviving descendants gathered at the hall. Beat: the unsaid inventory read aloud at last.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence, Part Two
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Among the descendants, an old woman supplies the missing context: the sentence addresses not the soldiers but the child — Ada herself. It means, roughly, 'You will carry us, and carrying us will be your home.' Beat: translation arrives through community, not scholarship.

chapters.title: Deathbed Grammar
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Ada is dying. Jonah speaks the sentence back to her in Nsibidi-Olum, flawed but hers, and adds the reply her mother never heard: that he carried it, and it held him. She dies mid-smile. Beat: catharsis.

chapters.title: Inventory Closed
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Aftermath: the estate agrees to a memorial and language archive; Charles, diminished, signs the deeds over the glasshouse to the descendants' trust. Jonah burns nothing and files nothing — the ledger of unsaid things is empty. Beat: reckoning without vengeance.

chapters.title: Tuning the Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Weeks later, Jonah tunes the conservatory piano for the first lesson taught by the new speakers — three descendants, children among them. The radiators sing a different history now. Beat: quiet hope.

chapters.title: The Word for Home
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Jonah's POV. Jonah stays on as caretaker-tuner of the glasshouse, neither guest nor owner but something the language has a word for and English does not. Closing image: frost on the glass, warmth inside, a sentence kept alive by being said. Beat: belonging chosen, identity translated.
